# Yomu

> A Japanese reader at https://yomu.neorgon.com/: paste a line and it is split
> into words, with furigana over the kanji, a romaji line for how it is said
> (Genki's convention: sayoonara, sensee, watashi wa) and one for how it is
> spelled (sa-yo-u-na-ra), notes on the special sounds and the grammar in the
> line, and a table of its kanji. Everything runs in the browser from
> committed dictionary files. Any Neorgon site on the allowlist can embed it
> in an iframe and send it text over postMessage. Nothing is uploaded.

## What a reading contains

Each token has a kind (word, inflected, particle, copula, katakana, name,
number, punct, and a few more), its surface, its dictionary form, its reading
in hiragana, furigana per kanji where the data allows, its beats, and two
romaji lines:

- said: long vowels doubled only inside one morpheme (思う stays omou),
  particles は へ を read wa e o, n' before a vowel or y, never macrons
- spelled: kana by kana with a hyphen between beats; a kana and a small
  vowel are one beat and one syllable in both lines (フィレンツェ
  fi-re-n-tse, firentse)

A number and its counter are one number token read by rule, with the sound
changes between them: 三本 さんぼん, 一分 いっぷん, 十名 じゅうめい (名 counts
people), 何人 なんにん. The counters are listed in docs/ANALYZER.md. Where the
whole number is also a dictionary word read the same way, the token keeps
that word's gloss: 何名 "how many people", 何階 "what floor".

Sound notes: particle-wa, particle-e, particle-o, fossil-wa (こんにちは),
long-vowel, small-tsu, youon, dakuten, handakuten, n-assimilation, devoiced
(written s(u)kides(u)), ji-zu, foreign-sound, bar, repeat-mark,
special-reading (今日 read as a whole), counter-change (いっぷん).

Loanword rules, on katakana words: loan-vowel (a vowel after a final
consonant, shop ショップ), loan-double (ッ after a short vowel), loan-long (ー
for -er, -or, -ar and long vowels), loan-f (フ, ファ), loan-lr (l written with
the r column), loan-v (v with the b column), loan-th (th with s or z),
loan-si (シ, ティ, ディ), loan-wasei (made-in-Japan English), loan-short
(パソコン from personal computer). A katakana compound with no record of its
own is one token with parts (インフォームショップ: a guess + shop). A part no
record covers may carry soundsLike, the English word it sounds like
(インフォーム: inform), found by running the loanword rules backwards over the
English words JMdict glosses with, and offered only when clearly ahead: on
held-out JMdict loanwords it answered 39 in 100 and was right on 90 in 100 of
those. It is a guess from the sound, shown as one, and never a gloss: the
part's gloss stays null.

Grammar notes: every particle, the copula forms, polite and plain verb
endings, te-forms (te-kudasai, te-iru, te-shimau, te-miru), desire, potential,
passive, causative, volitional, imperative, the conditionals ば, たら, なら and
と, i-adjective forms, invitations and offers.

Words outside JMdict's common set and names are read only where the common
words leave a guess: a rare word is marked as one (entry.tier 2), and a name
JMnedict knows is a name token with its reading; one it does not know is
still a guess, read from its kanji. A name written in katakana carries how it
is spelled in Latin letters, from JMnedict: token.name is { o: "Tom", types:
["given"] } for トム, and the Word panel says "Name: Tom (given name)". The
Word panel labels a rare word as one ("Rare word": not among the common
words, read from the full dictionary).
Records of borrowed words carry where they came from (ls, e.g. ["ger",
"Arbeit"]) and whether they were made in Japan (ws).

## Where the words part: Gaps

Japanese is written with no spaces. Display: Gaps (Off by default, On; saved
with the other preferences) draws a gap at every edge between two words of
the reading, and a hairline between the parts of a katakana compound
(テニス|トーナメント). A gap is a width and a line, never a typed space:
copying the reading copies no space it adds. Each gap carries one short
reason, decided by js/gaps.js from the analysis alone (token kinds, parts,
confidence and the characters), the first that holds of:

- particle or copula: the word after the edge, or before it, is a particle
  (は, を, か) or a form of the copula (です, だ)
- name: the word on either side is a name the dictionary knows
- script: the script changes across the edge (hiragana to kanji, ...); never
  before a kana no word starts with, where the edge is the reading guessing
- loan: katakana on both sides, and the word before ends the way a loanword
  does, ド, ト, ス, ク, グ or ル after a consonant sound (クレアディルド|オナニー,
  ゴールド|カード)
- nostart: the word before ends in katakana ン, ッ, ー or a small kana, which
  no word starts with, so the word ran on through it to the edge
  (ラーメン|ショップ). Not hiragana ん: the explanatory ん is a word of its
  own (登る|ん|です)
- guess: the word before has no dictionary word behind it, or the word after
  starts with a kana no word starts with (す|ご|ー|いね)
- compound: two plain parts of one katakana word
- word: the word before is a dictionary word (a form of one, a number and its
  counter, or a prefix such as お the dictionary lists on its own)

Whatever reason wins, a gap a guessed word touches is drawn dashed and its
reason ends "; the reading here is a guess". A pointer over a gap shows its
reason beside it, a tap on one pins it (until a tap elsewhere, Escape, a
resize or a new reading), and the Word panel lists the reasons of the gaps
before, inside and after the chosen word, in text, which is how a keyboard or
a screen reader reaches them; where there is no gap it says what stands there
(the line's start or end, punctuation, a space, Latin letters). A gap stays
on the row of the word it follows.
The first time Gaps is turned on, a one-line hint under the Display row says
what the gaps mean.

The full contract, including the token shape, is docs/ANALYZER.md in the
repository: https://github.com/energon-a-secas/yomu-site

## Embedding Yomu: yomu-embed/1

Frame URL: https://yomu.neorgon.com/?embed=1&lang=en (or lang=es). A top-level
page with ?embed=1 shows the normal site, because a frame with no host would
have nothing to read.

Text never travels in the frame URL. Every message is { v: 1, type, ... }.
A host that wants the on-device Translation inside the frame adds
allow="translator" to its iframe; without it the frame says the browser
cannot translate there.

Host to Yomu:

- yomu:hello (no fields): post it on the iframe's load event; Yomu can be
  ready before the host listens
- yomu:load { text, lang? }: read this text, at most 2,000 characters
- yomu:lang { lang }: switch the interface language

Yomu to host:

- yomu:ready { version }: on boot and in reply to every hello
- yomu:height { height }: the document height in CSS pixels, at most once per
  animation frame, so the host can size the frame
- yomu:read { tokens, unknown }: a load finished; unknown counts the tokens
  with no dictionary support
- yomu:error { message }: a load could not be read
- yomu:escape (no fields): Escape was pressed inside the frame; a host that
  shows Yomu in a closable sheet closes it

Yomu accepts messages only from https://runcible.neorgon.com and Runcible's
development server (http://localhost:8878, http://127.0.0.1:8878), checks
that the message came from its parent window, and posts only to the origin of
the last accepted hello. A new host is added to js/embed.js and docs/EMBED.md
in the same commit.

The embedded page keeps its text box, so a host that opens Yomu as a page of
its own (no text sent) still lets the learner paste.

## Linking to Yomu with text

https://yomu.neorgon.com/#t=<encodeURIComponent(text)> reads the text once and
then removes the fragment. Build this only for text you authored (a lesson's
phrase), never for text a person typed.

## Privacy

The pasted text is kept in this browser's localStorage under
yomu-site:text so a reload keeps it, with a visible Clear. A text is kept
under yomu-site:history only while the learner has Remember on (asked once,
after the first read; off until they say yes), up to 300 of them, for
History and "You read this before", or when the learner saved it on purpose
with the bookmark beside Clear, up to 500, whatever Remember says; turning
Remember off forgets every text not saved. No text is ever put in the URL,
an attribute, the page title or the beacon. The DeepL and Google Translate links are built at the moment
they are clicked, which is the only way the text in the box leaves the page.

Signing in is optional (one Neorgon account, the Neorgon Auth Kit; the
header's Sign in). Without it, everything below stays in this browser and
the page makes no request to Clerk, Convex or esm.sh. Signed in, Yomu keeps
a copy in that account, on Convex, so every device signed in has it: My
kanji (the saved kanji with their review schedules, and for every kanji met
its count, first and last day, up to eight dictionary words, the kind of
text and the History key it was last met in), the saved phrases (each one's
text, counts and times), Play's best scores, rounds and mixed-up pairs, and
the display choices language, furigana, romaji, highlights, the
unsaved-kanji mark and slow speech. Never sent: the text in the box, the
History texts not saved, the Remember and translation choices, and the
reading session. Unsaving a kanji or a phrase, and Clear all of My kanji,
reach the other devices; the account keeps the removal (a time and a key),
never the text of an unsaved phrase. Signing out stops syncing and keeps
everything in the browser. An embedded Yomu never starts sign-in.

The Translation under the reading uses the browser's own on-device
Translator API (Chrome 138+ and Edge on a computer): after the learner clicks
Translate here once, the browser downloads a Japanese model and translates on
the device, so the text is not sent anywhere; the translation is held in
memory only. Other browsers say so and keep the two links. A translation
that gets no answer and no download progress for 20 seconds, or that the
browser refuses, ends in a line saying why and a Try again button.

## My kanji

https://yomu.neorgon.com/#/kanji is a screen of the kanji a learner saved for
review, with a review at #/kanji/review, the collection at
#/kanji/collection and History at #/kanji/history. In the reader, each kanji
in the kanji table and in the Word panel has a save toggle, each row says how
many texts the kanji was met in (with a New chip the first time), and kanji
not saved yet carry a small folded corner (Display: Unsaved kanji, Mark or
Off). An embedded Yomu has a My kanji link in its one-line bar, and a text
the host sends always opens the reader.

- Times seen counts texts: a kanji counts once per reading session, and a
  session begins when the box gets a new text at once (an example, a phrase,
  a #t= link, yomu:load, or a paste into an empty box or over all of it) or
  after it is emptied. A paste added to the text already there, and a
  reload, count nothing again.
- Review: Show, then Again (box 1, due tomorrow, and again before the review
  ends) or Got it (next box, due in 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 days). Keys: Space, 1, 2,
  Escape.
- Collection: every kanji read is collected. The shelves are the 2,136 jōyō
  kanji by school grade (1 to 6, then secondary school), from
  data/kanji/joyo.json (yomu-joyo/1), plus an Extra shelf for the rest. A
  read that collects a kanji for the first time says so in a toast, with the
  jōyō count and any milestone (a grade complete, 100 jōyō kanji).
- Where each kanji was last met: the kind of text (pasted, typed, an
  example, a phrase, a link, a text Runcible sent, History), and, with
  Remember on or when that text is saved, the sentence it was in.
- History (opt-in): with Remember on, each text read, how often, first and
  last, with Read again and Forget, and "You read this before" (or "This is
  part of a text you read") in the reader.
- Saved phrases: the bookmark beside Clear, or on a History row, saves the
  text on purpose, whatever Remember says (with it off, that text and no
  other is kept). A saved text is listed first in History ("Saved phrases"),
  is counted again when read again with "You read this before", is never
  evicted by the 300-text cap, survives Forget all and Turn off, and is
  forgotten only when unsaved with Remember off. At most 500.
- Kept in this browser's localStorage under yomu-site:kanji: each saved
  kanji's schedule, and for each kanji met, how often, the first and last day,
  up to eight dictionary words with their readings, the kind of text it was
  last met in, and with Remember on or a saved text a key (a hash) of that
  text; and the reading session in progress (the kanji counted in it, and
  when it began). Never the text: that is only in yomu-site:history. Signed
  in, the same fields (not the session) also sync to the account (Privacy).
- Export writes a yomu-kanji-export/1 JSON file ({ format, exported, saved,
  seen, phrases? }); Import validates one and merges it, keeping the higher
  counts and the earlier first day. `phrases` is the saved phrases only
  ([{ t, first, last, n, src, saved }]), written when there is one; a file
  without it imports as before. The rest of History is not exported.

## Play

https://yomu.neorgon.com/#/play holds five short games: four with the
characters that look alike, each a round of ten (keys 1 to 4 answer, Enter or
Space goes on, Escape leaves), with the right answer marked and a one-line
reason after each, and a result with the best score and the pairs mixed up,
each kanji with its save toggle, and one with where the words part:

- Which one? (#/play/which): the kana for a romaji among its look-alikes
  (twenty sets of hiragana and katakana, each kana with a hint written for
  Yomu), or the kanji for its meanings and a reading among the kanji that look
  like it, drawn from the learner's collection, or the 1st and 2nd grade
  while that holds fewer than ten.
- Odd one out (#/play/odd): a grid of one character hiding one look-alike,
  4x4 growing to 6x6; 60 seconds with a wrong tap costing 3, or ten grids
  untimed (the default when the device asks for reduced motion). The clock
  stands still while the game is not on screen (the page hidden, scrolled
  away, or a host's sheet closed over the frame), and a round never ends
  while it is.
- Twins across scripts (#/play/twins): へ/ヘ, カ/力, エ/工, ロ/口, ニ/二, タ/夕,
  ト/卜, ハ/八, オ/才, り/リ and ー/一, told apart by the word around them.
- Name decoder (#/play/names): a katakana name, said to be a name or a
  place, and four original spellings of that class; the answer spells it
  kana by kana (ト-ム, to-mu: Tom). It reads data/names/popular.json
  (yomu-names-popular/1) and says it is not available until that file
  ships.
- Where are the spaces? (#/play/spaces, ¿Dónde van los espacios?): a line
  with no gaps, and a toggle at every place between two characters; the
  learner marks where each word ends and checks. Missed and extra spaces are
  marked, and each space of the answer shows its reason from Gaps. A line
  scores the spaces placed right minus the extras, never below 0; a round is
  ten lines, the hiragana ones first (the particles are the clue), then
  lines with kanji and katakana, then katakana compounds. Keys: the arrows
  move between the places, Space marks one, Enter checks, then Enter or
  Space goes on, Escape leaves. The answer key is Yomu's own analysis of
  each line, emitted with the lines as data/play/spaces.json
  (yomu-spaces/1) by tools/build-spaces.mjs: the phrase library's lines, cut
  into sentences, as written and spelled in hiragana from the library's own
  kana, and twelve lines written for Yomu around a katakana compound (the
  library has none). A line is left out when its reading disagrees with the
  library's kana, when it is or holds a set phrase the analysis cuts inside,
  when a prefix stands as a word of its own, when the analysis does not
  settle where its words part (two neighbouring tokens that are one
  dictionary word, 卵|焼き; a counter that runs on into the next word, 何番|線;
  a word that ends in a particle, 何と in 何と言いますか; one token that is
  two words, 待っています, お願いします), when its kana spelling parts where
  the kanji do not or reads a word as another word (いって as 要る), when it
  holds a guess, or when it has no space to find. On 2026-10-07: 121 lines,
  67 of the library's 151 sentences as written, 42 in hiragana and 12
  compound lines; tiers 48, 61 and 12. The hint over a line with kanji or
  katakana names the scripts it holds.

The kanji look-alikes are data/play/lookalikes.json (yomu-lookalikes/1): for
each jōyō kanji that has any, at most five, best first, chosen by rule from
the KanjiVG parts and KANJIDIC stroke counts of the kanji shards, plus
authored classic pairs (土 士, 己 已 巳, 日 曰, ...); on 60 pairs drawn at
random, 58 were ones a learner would confuse at a glance. Kept in this
browser's localStorage under yomu-site:play: each game's best score and
number of rounds (the spaces game's best in points), and how often each pair
of characters was mixed up, so a pair mixed up comes round more often. No
text is kept. Signed in, the scores and pairs also sync to the account
(Privacy).

## Data and licences

- JMdict and KANJIDIC, by the Electronic Dictionary Research and Development
  Group, CC BY-SA 4.0: the glosses, readings and kanji information
- JMnedict, by the same Group, CC BY-SA 4.0: the readings and types of the
  surnames, given names and place names a text may hold, and the Latin
  spelling of a name written in katakana. data/names/popular.json
  (yomu-names-popular/1) lists the katakana names the corpus uses most, each
  as [katakana, Latin spelling, given | surname | person | place, sentence
  count], for a game; the type is that of the JMnedict sense the spelling
  comes from, or person for a place the corpus uses as one (Mr. Smith,
  スミスさん, Gogh painted), or place for a name it uses as a place and
  JMnedict types a place too (from Milan, Mt. Everest), or, for the few
  names no evidence reaches, a class written for Yomu (Romeo is a person);
  it carries the same licence block
- KanjiVG, by Ulrich Apel, CC BY-SA 3.0: the parts of each kanji
- Tatoeba, CC BY 2.0 FR: used only to rank how common each word is, to
  choose and count names, and, through the English translations of its
  Japanese sentences, to choose which JMnedict spelling of a katakana name
  is shown (ジョン John, not Jon) and whether the game calls it a name or a
  place; no sentence ships
- The phrase library, the notes, the deinflection rules, and Play's hints,
  example words, look-alike rules, the Name decoder's few authored name
  classes and the spaces game's compound lines are written for Yomu and are
  public domain. Where a line's words part is Yomu's reading of it over
  JMdict and JMnedict, so data/play/spaces.json carries their licence block. Nothing is taken from Genki, the Japan
  Foundation apps, Tofugu, Yomitan, rikaichan or 10ten.
